title: The general and special linear group schemes
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $c\geq1$. Put $P=k[x_{ij}:1\leq i,j\leq c]$, the multivariate polynomial algebra [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], and $X=(x_{ij})$, a matrix [def-weil-matrix]. With determinant as in [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], put
$$D=\det X=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_c}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^c x_{i\sigma(i)},\qquad A=P[1/D]$$
using localization [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. The *general linear group scheme* is $\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], a group scheme in [def-sc-group-scheme], with coordinate $k$-algebra maps
$$m^*(x_{ij})=\sum_{r=1}^c x_{ir}\otimes x_{rj},\qquad\varepsilon(x_{ij})=\delta_{ij},\qquad i^*(x_{ij})=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ji}/D.$$
Here tensor products are commutative $k$-algebra tensor products [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]; $M_{ji}$ is the determinant of the submatrix obtained by deleting row $j$ and column $i$ of $X$. For $c=1$ that minor is the empty determinant $1$. The values on $D^{-1}$ are forced by those on $x_{ij}$. For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient], its $R$-points (morphisms $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}$ over $\operatorname{Spec}k$) identify naturally with the group of invertible $c\times c$ matrices over $R$, with multiplication $(UV)_{ij}=\sum_rU_{ir}V_{rj}$, identity $(\delta_{ij})$, and matrix inverse.

The *special linear group scheme* is
$$\mathrm{SL}_{c,k}=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(P/(D-1)\bigr)\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{c,k},$$
where the quotient algebra is as in [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The inclusion is induced by $A\to P/(D-1)$ sending $x_{ij}$ to its residue class and $D^{-1}$ to $1$; it is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] and a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Its $R$-points are the matrices with determinant $1$. Finally the determinant is a homomorphism $\det:\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}\to\mathbf G_m$ [def-sc-gm-ga], dual to the $k$-algebra map $k[t,t^{-1}]\to A$ with $t\mapsto D$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] with $m=n=c$. The only subset of $\{1,\ldots,c\}$ of size $c$ is the whole set, whose submatrices are the original matrices. Thus $\det(UV)=\det(U)\det(V)$ over every commutative ring. From [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], $\det I=1$: only the identity permutation contributes. Applying a ring homomorphism to the finite Leibniz sum proves $f(\det U)=\det(f(U))$. The row-indexed Leibniz formula used here agrees with that node's column-indexed formula by replacing $\sigma$ with $\sigma^{-1}$, whose sign is the same and whose factors are a reindexing of the product.

source.place: Tag 0F0K (item-cauchy-binet), square specialization; Leibniz calculations supplied

proof.text: For any $c\times c$ matrix $U$ over a commutative ring with $d=\det U$ a unit, [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-adjugate-identity] gives both $U(d^{-1}\operatorname{adj}U)=I$ and $(d^{-1}\operatorname{adj}U)U=I$. Conversely an inverse $V$ gives $\det U\det V=\det V\det U=1$ by Step 1. This proves the equivalence of invertibility and unit determinant, and the inverse-entry formula. A two-sided inverse is unique: if $UV=VU=I$ and $UW=WU=I$, then $V=V(UW)=(VU)W=W$. The matrix associativity used here is a finite-sum identity: both $((UV)W)_{ij}$ and $(U(VW))_{ij}$ are $\sum_{r,s}U_{ir}V_{rs}W_{sj}$. Identity multiplication follows by summing the Kronecker deltas.

source.place: Tag 07DQ (lemma-matrix-left-inverse), proof: the two adjugate identities; elementary consequences written out

proof.text: By [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], a $k$-algebra map $P\to R$ is uniquely a choice of entries $u_{ij}\in R$. Its value at $D$ is $\det U$ by Step 1. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property] to $\{1,D,D^2,\ldots\}$. It extends uniquely to $A\to R$ exactly when $\det U$ is a unit; the extension takes $f/D^n$ to $f(U)(\det U)^{-n}$. It is a $k$-algebra map since it agrees with the original map on constants. Step 2 identifies these tuples with invertible matrices. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum] these maps are exactly the $R$-points over $\operatorname{Spec}k$. This bijection commutes with every $k$-algebra map $R\to R'$ since applying that map to the entries gives the same evaluation on every polynomial and every inverse denominator. In particular, maps from $A$ are determined by the coordinate entries.

source.place: Tag 022W (example-general-linear-group), representability; localization justified by algebra.tex, Tag 00CP (proposition-universal-property-localization)

proof.text: Set $A=P[1/D]$ using [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. In the commutative algebra $A\otimes_k A$ of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property], let $X_L=(x_{ij}\otimes1)$ and $X_R=(1\otimes x_{ij})$. Their determinants are $D\otimes1$ and $1\otimes D$, both units, by Step 1. Hence $X_LX_R$ is invertible, and Step 3 constructs the algebra map $m^*:A\to A\otimes_k A$ with the claimed coordinate values. Evaluating at $I$ gives $\varepsilon:A\to k$. In $A$, Step 2 gives $Y=D^{-1}\operatorname{adj}X$ with $XY=YX=I$, so $\det Y=D^{-1}$ by Step 1. Evaluation at $Y$ gives $i^*:A\to A$, whose entries are exactly the signed transposed minors in the statement. These are actual algebra maps, including on inverse denominators. The spectrum correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and the affine-product formula [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] turn them into $m,i,e$ on the displayed affine scheme.

source.place: Tag 022W (example-general-linear-group), multiplication formula; current blueprint companion proof for identity and inverse

proof.text: Check the diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] on coordinates, using Step 3 to detect equality of maps from $A$. The tensor universal property [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property] identifies either parenthesization of the triple product by $(a\otimes b)\otimes c\leftrightarrow a\otimes(b\otimes c)$. Both iterated multiplications send $x_{ij}$ to $\sum_{r,s}x_{ir}\otimes x_{rs}\otimes x_{sj}$. The two unit composites take $x_{ij}$ to $\sum_r\delta_{ir}x_{rj}=x_{ij}$ and $\sum_rx_{ir}\delta_{rj}=x_{ij}$. For the two inverse diagrams, the tensor maps $a\otimes b\mapsto i^*(a)b$ and $a\otimes b\mapsto ai^*(b)$ exist by the same universal property, and their composites with $m^*$ take $x_{ij}$ to $(YX)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ and $(XY)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ by Step 2. These are the values of the identity section followed by the structural map. By the affine-product formula [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] the iterated products of $\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}$ are the spectra of these tensor algebras, with the projections induced by the coordinate inclusions, so $m\times\mathrm{id}$, $\mathrm{id}\times m$, $(i,\mathrm{id})$ and $(\mathrm{id},i)$ are the spectra of the maps above. Thus the diagrams commute as scheme morphisms by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Evaluation of $m^*$, $\varepsilon$ and $i^*$ at any $R$ gives precisely matrix product, identity and inverse. The natural bijection in Step 3 is therefore a group isomorphism.

source.place: entire proof paragraph, associativity, unit and inverse calculations expanded

proof.text: For $\mathbf G_m$ as in [def-sc-gm-ga], send $\sum_na_nt^n\in k[t,t^{-1}]$ to $\sum_na_nD^n\in A$. This is an algebra map: finite sums and convolution of exponents preserve addition and multiplication, and $D$ is a unit. Thus it defines the claimed determinant morphism by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Step 1 applied to $X_LX_R$ gives $m^*(D)=(D\otimes1)(1\otimes D)=D\otimes D$; also $\varepsilon(D)=1$ and $i^*(D)=D^{-1}$. These are exactly the multiplication, identity and inverse formulas for $t$ in [def-sc-gm-ga]; equality on $t$ forces equality on $t^{-1}$ and on every Laurent polynomial. Hence the determinant is a homomorphism in [def-sc-group-scheme], with value $\det U$ on the matrix point $U$.

source.place: Tag 022X (example-determinant), expanded using the coordinate formulas of Tag 022U (example-multiplicative-group)

proof.text: Let $Q=P/(D-1)$ with residue matrix $\bar X$. The quotient map is surjective and $\det\bar X=1$ by [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient] and Step 1. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property] extends it to $q:A\to Q$ with $q(D^{-1})=1$. It remains surjective, since each residue polynomial is the image of the same polynomial in $A$. More precisely $A/(D-1)A\cong Q$: $q$ induces one map, and $P\to A/(D-1)A$ induces the other since it kills $D-1$. The composites fix every coordinate; they also fix the inverse of $D$, which equals $1$ in these quotients, so they are identities. Therefore $\operatorname{Spec}q$ is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]: apply [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-affine-cover-criterion](2) to the covering of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ by the single affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A$, whose preimage $\operatorname{Spec}Q$ is affine with surjective section map $q$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. A map $Q\to R$ is exactly evaluation at entries $U$ with $\det U=1$: substitutions killing $D-1$ factor by $[f]\mapsto f(U)$, well-defined since every multiple of $D-1$ evaluates to zero. This proves the asserted image on $R$-points, with no reducedness assumption on $R$.

source.place: special-linear quotient clause, omitted algebra verification supplied; closed immersions: morphisms.tex, Tag 01QO (lemma-closed-immersion)

proof.text: In $Q\otimes_kQ$, the two generic residue matrices have determinant $1$, so their product also has determinant $1$ by Step 1. Substitution therefore defines $Q\to Q\otimes_kQ$; evaluation at $I$ defines $Q\to k$. In $Q$, Step 2 gives $\bar X^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}\bar X$, and Step 1 gives its determinant $1$, so substitution also defines $Q\to Q$ for the inverse. Factorization through $P/(D-1)$ is the representative calculation of Step 7. Under the affine-product formula [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] these are group operations, since the coordinate identities of Step 5 remain valid after taking residue classes; the inclusion preserves the operations because its pullback $q$ preserves each displayed coordinate formula. On every $R$ it is injective: two maps $Q\to R$ agreeing after the surjection $q$ agree on every residue polynomial. Its image is the matrices with determinant $1$, containing $I$ and closed under product and inverse by Step 1. This verifies exactly the closed-subgroup condition [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] and all the special-linear clauses.

source.place: special-linear closed-subgroup clause, group operations and subgroup verification supplied

blueprint_update.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $c\geq1$. The *general linear group
scheme* is the affine scheme

$$
\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}:=\Spec k[x_{ij}:1\leq i,j\leq c]\bigl[1/\det\bigr],
\qquad
\det:=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_c}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
\prod_{i=1}^{c}x_{i\sigma(i)},
$$

with comultiplication $m^*(x_{ij})=\sum_{r=1}^{c}x_{ir}\otimes x_{rj}$,
counit $\varepsilon(x_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$ and antipode
$i^*(x_{ij})=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ji}/\det$, where $M_{ji}$ is the
determinant of the matrix obtained from $(x_{kl})$ by deleting row
$j$ and column $i$, as a group scheme in the sense of
[def-sc-group-scheme]. Its $R$-points are
$\mathrm{GL}_c(R)$, the group of invertible $c\times c$ matrices over
$R$. The *special linear group scheme* is the closed
subgroup scheme

$$
\mathrm{SL}_{c,k}:=\Spec k[x_{ij}]/(\det-1)\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}.
$$

The determinant defines a homomorphism
$\det:\mathrm{GL}_{c,k}\to\mathbf G_m$ with
[def-sc-gm-ga], dual to $t\mapsto\det$.

proof.text:
The group-scheme axioms of [def-sc-group-scheme] hold because matrix
multiplication is associative, $1$ is a unit and
$A\cdot A^{\mathrm{adj}}=\det(A)\cdot1$ with $A^{\mathrm{adj}}=\bigl((-1)^{k+l}M_{lk}\bigr)_{k,l}$. The
determinant is a homomorphism because $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.
